y-m-74-01.topic: Classifying by nearest neighbor: distance and units
y-m-74-01.material:
A fruit-sorting app classifies a new fruit as either 'apple' or 'pear'. The method is 'follow the nearest neighbor'. Among the fruits whose names are known, it finds the fruit closest in distance to the new fruit and gives the new fruit that fruit's name.
The distance between two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is measured as √((x1−x2)²+(y1−y2)²). (√ is read as 'root'.)
Fruits whose names are known (two features: weight [g], sweetness [a number in Brix units; the bigger, the sweeter])
- Fruit P: apple, weight 154g, sweetness 12
- Fruit R: pear, weight 165g, sweetness 16
New fruit Q: weight 172g, sweetness 12
Assumption: the numbers of the two features are put into the distance calculation as they are.
y-m-74-01.thinking.2: Finding the hidden assumption that the distance standard creates
y-m-74-01.prereq.0: The H1 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Only content up to middle-school math is assumed.
y-m-74-01.prereq.1: Reading and calculating the distance √((horizontal difference)²+(vertical difference)²) between two points on a coordinate plane (middle-school level)
y-m-74-01.s.s1.prompt: If distance is measured with weight in g and sweetness as the Brix number as is, how will Q be classified?
y-m-74-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write down separately the weight difference and the sweetness difference for Q and P, and for Q and R.
y-m-74-01.s.s1.hint.1: Put the two distances side by side and compare which is smaller.
y-m-74-01.s.s1.explain: The distance between Q and P is √(18²+0²)=18, and the distance between Q and R is √(7²+4²)=√65≈8.1. In this unit R is closer, so Q is classified as a pear.
y-m-74-01.s.s3.hint.0: Recall how the distances differ in each of the two cases, g and kg.
y-m-74-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what would be good to do so that the numbers of the two features take a similar share of the distance.
y-m-74-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: When the unit changes ... so ...

y-m-74-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does it include a thought about which of weight and sweetness is more important for classification?
y-m-74-01.s.s3.model.1: We first have to decide which of weight and sweetness is more important. When the unit changes, the importance secretly changes, so let's either match them to the same standard regardless of units or decide the importance ourselves and use that.

y-m-74-02.title: If the learning rate η is large, will it arrive faster?
y-m-74-02.topic: Learning rate and convergence of gradient descent
y-m-74-02.goal: By making values yourself, check that if the size of each correction (the learning rate) is too large it overshoots the target, and that within a certain range it gets closer again even after overshooting, and explain why.
y-m-74-02.material:
'Learning' in an AI model is the work of finding the value w at which the loss (how wrong it is) becomes smallest. The loss in this task is L(w) = (w−3)², so it is smallest, 0, when w = 3.
The computer corrects w like this.
new w = current w − η × 2(w−3)
(η is the learning rate, read 'eta'. 2(w−3) is an expression, already given, for how the loss changes at the current w. You just substitute values and calculate.)
The starting w is 0, and η is greater than 0. Hajun, a friend in the club, said, "If I set η large, to 1, won't it arrive fastest in one go?"
y-m-74-02.thinking.0: Testing a friend's claim by substituting values
y-m-74-02.thinking.1: Finding several learning rates that meet the conditions
y-m-74-02.thinking.2: Explaining convergence by the change in distance
y-m-74-02.prereq.0: The H1 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Only content up to middle-school math is assumed.
y-m-74-02.prereq.1: Reading that the minimum of the quadratic function (w−3)² occurs at w=3 (middle-school level)
y-m-74-02.prereq.2: Substituting numbers into a linear expression and calculating
y-m-74-02.prereq.3: Showing distance with absolute value. Differentiation is not used: the 2(w−3) used in the correction formula is given.
y-m-74-02.s.s1.prompt: With η = 1, if you correct three times starting from w = 0, what does w become in turn?
y-m-74-02.s.s1.hint.0: Put the starting w = 0 into the formula to find the first value, then put that value back into the w place in the formula.
y-m-74-02.s.s1.hint.1: After each step, write down together whether w is greater or less than 3 and its distance from 3.
y-m-74-02.s.s1.o.a: 6, 0, 6 — it only jumps back and forth across 3
y-m-74-02.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment made by putting values into the formula at each correction. Also check whether there is any moment when it seems to arrive at 3.
y-m-74-02.s.s1.o.b: 6, 3, 3 — it arrives at 3 the second time and stays there
y-m-74-02.s.s1.r.b: Put in the second value yourself. You need to check whether correcting from 6 gives 3.
y-m-74-02.s.s1.o.c: 3, 3, 3 — it arrives at 3 right from the first correction
y-m-74-02.s.s1.r.c: Calculate the first corrected value yourself. You need to check whether the result of putting in the starting w of 0 is 3.
y-m-74-02.s.s1.o.d: 6, 12, 18 — it only keeps getting bigger and does not decrease
y-m-74-02.s.s1.r.d: You found the first value correctly, but you missed that in the calculation correcting again from 6, w moves in the direction of decreasing.
y-m-74-02.s.s1.explain: First: 0 − 1×2(0−3) = 6. Second: 6 − 1×2(6−3) = 0. Third: 0 − 1×2(0−3) = 6. With η = 1 it only jumps back and forth across 3 and does not get closer.
y-m-74-02.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different learning rates η for which w overshoots 3 once but gradually gets closer to 3. There are two conditions. (1) After correcting once from the starting w = 0, w is greater than 3. (2) After correcting twice, the distance between w and 3 is less than the starting distance of 3. (η is greater than 0.)
y-m-74-02.s.s2.hint.0: Pick an η, correct w twice yourself, and check each of the two conditions.
y-m-74-02.s.s2.hint.1: See which condition breaks at η = 1 and at η = 0.3, and move the value to somewhere between them.
y-m-74-02.s.s2.ok.c2: After one correction, w (=6η) is over 3.
y-m-74-02.s.s2.fail.c2: After one correction, w is not greater than 3. Calculate the w after one correction yourself.
y-m-74-02.s.s2.ok.c3: After two corrections, the distance from 3 is less than 3.
y-m-74-02.s.s2.fail.c3: After two corrections, the distance from 3 is not less than 3. Calculate the w after two corrections yourself.
y-m-74-02.s.s2.explain: With η = 0.6, w goes 0 → 3.6 → 2.88, passing over 3 and then getting close again. The η that meets the conditions of this task is a number between 0.5 and 1. With η = 1, even after two corrections the distance stays 3, so it does not meet the conditions.
y-m-74-02.s.s3.prompt: When η = 0.6, w gets closer to 3 even after passing it, but when η = 1, it does not get closer. Explain why by comparing how the distance from 3 changes with each correction.
y-m-74-02.s.s3.hint.0: In a table, write how far w is from 3 for η = 0.6 and for η = 1.
y-m-74-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the two cases for how many times the distance becomes with each correction.
y-m-74-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: When η = 0.6 the distance is ... and when η = 1 it is ...
y-m-74-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the numbers you used came from values actually corrected?
y-m-74-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare η = 0.6 and η = 1 by the same standard (distance)?
y-m-74-02.s.s3.model.0: When η = 0.6, the distance from 3 shrinks every time: 3 → 0.6 → 0.12. When η = 1, the distance stays 3 → 3 → 3, so it does not get closer.
y-m-74-02.s.s3.model.1: With each correction, the distance from 3 changes by a fixed ratio. At η = 0.6 that ratio is less than 1, so the distance shrinks, and at η = 1 the ratio is 1, so the distance stays the same. So 0.6 gets closer and 1 just circles in place.

y-m-74-03.title: What does the average menu number of 1.75 mean?
y-m-74-03.topic: A trap when storing categorical data as numbers
y-m-74-03.goal: Check by calculation that the average of numbers attached as labels changes depending on how the numbers are assigned, so it is not information about the menu, and write what should be said instead.
y-m-74-03.material:
The school app stores the 'favorite lunch menu' as a number. Gimbap = 1, ramyeon = 2, tteokbokki = 3, bibimbap = 4. 8 students answered; 6 chose gimbap, 2 chose bibimbap, and no student chose ramyeon or tteokbokki. The app screen shows "Average menu number: 1.75".
One team member said, "1.75 is between gimbap (1) and ramyeon (2), so the students in our school tend to like gimbap or ramyeon."
y-m-74-03.thinking.0: Evaluating whether a value stored as a number means size
y-m-74-03.thinking.1: Changing the numbers and recalculating with the same data
y-m-74-03.thinking.2: Thinking of other ways to represent categorical data
y-m-74-03.prereq.0: The H1 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Only content up to middle-school math is assumed.
y-m-74-03.prereq.1: Calculating the mean: (sum of value × number of students) ÷ total number of students (middle-school level)
y-m-74-03.prereq.2: Counting heads and organizing them in a table
y-m-74-03.s.s1.prompt: What is the best evaluation of this team member's interpretation?
y-m-74-03.s.s1.hint.0: Count in a table whether any students actually chose ramyeon (2) or tteokbokki (3).
y-m-74-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what would happen to the results of the same students if the numbers were assigned in a different order.
y-m-74-03.s.s1.o.a: Right. The average reflects all the answers evenly, so 1.75 shows the center of preference.
y-m-74-03.s.s1.r.a: It is true that the average uses all the values, but that is for the case when the values are numbers with size. You did not ask whether the numbers here mean size.
y-m-74-03.s.s1.o.b: Not right. The numbers are only menu labels, so the average does not mean 'between menus'.
y-m-74-03.s.s1.r.b: This is a judgment that treats the numbers as labels. It becomes firmer if you check what happens when the numbers are assigned differently.
y-m-74-03.s.s1.o.c: Right. It was calculated exactly to two decimal places, so 1.75 is a value you can trust.
y-m-74-03.s.s1.r.c: A calculation being exact and the value having a meaning are different things. You should ask what the exactly calculated number represents.
y-m-74-03.s.s1.o.d: Can't tell. 8 students is too few, so this is data from which an average cannot even be taken.
y-m-74-03.s.s1.r.d: An average can be calculated even with few people. The problem is not the number of people but what the numbers being averaged mean.
y-m-74-03.s.s1.explain: The numbers are labels attached to tell the menus apart, so the average of the numbers, 1.75, does not mean 'a menu close to ramyeon'. In fact, not a single student chose ramyeon.
y-m-74-03.s.s2.prompt: Store the numbers changed to gimbap = 4 and bibimbap = 1 (ramyeon = 2 and tteokbokki = 3 stay the same), and find the average for the same 8 students again. What is the average?
y-m-74-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write down the number held by the 6 students and the number held by the 2 students.
y-m-74-03.s.s2.hint.1: First find the sum of the 8 changed numbers, and see why that sum changes.
y-m-74-03.s.s2.r.a: 6 students have 4 and 2 students have 1, so the sum is 26, and the average is that divided by 8. You confirmed that for the same students the average changed a lot.
y-m-74-03.s.s2.r.b: You assumed that because only the numbers were changed, the average stays the same. Write down again what number the 6 students have now.
y-m-74-03.s.s2.r.c: You found the middle value of the changed numbers 1 and 4. You need to reflect how many students each number has (6 and 2).
y-m-74-03.s.s2.r.d: You took the number of the menu that the most people chose to be the average. The average is calculated by reflecting every student's number.
y-m-74-03.s.s2.explain: (6×4 + 2×1) ÷ 8 = 26 ÷ 8 = 3.25. The same 8 students chose the same menus, but the average number changed from 1.75 to 3.25. The average is a value that comes from how the numbers were assigned, not from the students' minds.
y-m-74-03.s.s3.prompt: The average changed depending on how the numbers were assigned. Write, with reasons, what and how you should say to report the students' preferences with numbers in this data.
y-m-74-03.s.s3.hint.0: Think of two different ways to describe the answers of the same 8 students with numbers.
y-m-74-03.s.s3.hint.1: Look for a value that does not change however the numbers are assigned.
y-m-74-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: I will say it with ... because ...
y-m-74-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the value I want to report stay the same even if the numbers are changed?
y-m-74-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does the method I used instead of the average reflect the choices of all 8 students?
y-m-74-03.s.s3.model.0: It is better to count how many chose each menu and say 'gimbap 6 students, bibimbap 2 students, gimbap is the most'. The numbers are labels, so if the numbers change the average changes, so the average can't be used.
y-m-74-03.s.s3.model.1: I will not use the average of the numbers and will show the share for each menu instead. Gimbap 75%, bibimbap 25%. The numbers have no meaning as order or size, so they should not be added and divided.

y-m-74-04.title: If it was 95% with photos taken the same way, will it be 95% in the collection bin too?
y-m-74-04.topic: Representativeness of the training data and interpreting test results
y-m-74-04.goal: Check with new data that the meaning of accuracy changes depending on whether the data used for the test are the same kind as the real use, and revise the judgment and the degree of confidence to choose an honest reporting sentence.
y-m-74-04.material: The recycling helper app team made an AI that sorts container photos into one of 'plastic', 'can', or 'glass'. The 2,000 training photos were all clean new containers taken on a white desk. The 200 test photos were taken the same way. (The test photos are photos not used in training.) Accuracy is the number of photos correct divided by the total number of photos (as a percentage).
y-m-74-04.thinking.0: Revising judgment and confidence to fit new data
y-m-74-04.thinking.1: Interpreting accuracy together with which data it was obtained from
y-m-74-04.thinking.2: Comparing which of several improvement directions are reasonable
y-m-74-04.prereq.0: The H1 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Only content up to middle-school math is assumed.
y-m-74-04.prereq.1: Reading accuracy = number correct ÷ total number as a percentage
y-m-74-04.prereq.2: Knowing that the data used for training and the data used for testing are different
y-m-74-04.s.s1.prompt: The data are revealed one piece at a time. Choose a judgment each time.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first write down where and how the photos used in the test were taken.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.hint.1: Tell whether the newly learned number changes the judgment or changes only the degree of confidence.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Of the 200 test photos, 190 were correct. The accuracy is 95%. The team says, "Let's install it in the school recycling bins right away."
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Will it get about 95% right with photos taken at the recycling bin too?
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.after: The test photos were taken the same way as the training photos. So the 95% is a value for 'photos of clean new containers taken on a desk', and at the bin it could be different.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It will be around 95%, because the test photos are photos not used in training.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Separating the test photos from training is good. But you must separately ask whether the test photos are the same kind as the photos that will actually be used.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It could be lower. We do not know whether the real photos are the same kind as the test photos.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You pointed out that it has not been confirmed whether the tested photos and the photos to be used are the same kind.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We cannot know, so this 95% gives no information at all.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It is correct that it is information about performance on photos taken the same way. That means we must not speak beyond that range, not that it is useless.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It will be higher than 95%, because the more training photos, the higher the accuracy.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: More photos may help, but unless you change what kind of photos they are, you cannot know the performance on real photos.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.info: We tested with 100 photos taken at the recycling bin and got 78 right (78%). Many of the containers photographed were crushed, had labels on, or were wet.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: What is the most fitting way to interpret the difference between 95% and 78%?
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.after: The 78% from the bin photos is from 100 photos, so it can wobble by a few %p, but the large gap from 95% has to be read together with the clue that the kind of photos was different. A value obtained from the same kind of photos as where it will actually be used is the more fitting evidence.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The 78% came out by chance, so we keep trusting the original 95%.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: A 17%p gap with 100 photos looks too big to explain by chance alone. There is also the clue that the kind of photos was different.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The average of the two accuracies, about 86.5%, can be taken as the true performance.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Averaging two values from different kinds of photos does not represent either situation. You must pick the value that matches the situation of use.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It dropped because the kind of photos was different. 78% is closer to real use.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You chose the value from the side where the tested photos are closer to real use. The first judgment gained concrete evidence.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: There are only 100, so even 78% can't be trusted, and we make no judgment at all.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: With 100 photos, 78% can wobble by a few %p. Still, that does not erase the large gap from 95%.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Looking at the 22 wrong photos, 20 were photos of containers that were crushed, labeled, or wet, and 2 were photos of clean containers.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Choose what the team should do next. (More than one may be fitting.)
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.after: 20 of the 22 wrong photos were containers that were crushed, labeled, or wet. Both adding that kind to the training (c) and narrowing the app's conditions of use to that range and testing again (d) are reasonable.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Take 2,000 more photos on the desk the same way and train on them
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The number grew, but the kind of photos stays the same. It does not match what kind the wrong photos were.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Remove the 22 wrong bin photos, recalculate the accuracy, and announce it
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If you remove wrong photos, every model's accuracy goes up. It changes the test result, so the performance cannot be reported.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Add photos of crushed and labeled containers to the training data and train again
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a way of adding the kind found as the reason for the errors to the training data. It is necessary to check again with new test photos.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Put a note in the app saying 'Please rinse the container, flatten it, and photograph it', and test again under that condition
y-m-74-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a way of setting the conditions of use and testing under those conditions. It is a design that fits the range of use without changing the model.
y-m-74-04.s.s1.reflect: How did your judgment and confidence change between when you first heard 95% and after you saw the bin photo results? Why must you write 'what photos it was tested with' together with the accuracy?
y-m-74-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose every sentence for the presentation that fits the facts and does not exaggerate.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.hint.0: For each sentence, check whether it says 'what photos it was tested with'.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the range each sentence speaks of (these 100 photos, or all bins).
y-m-74-04.s.s2.o.a: The accuracy of the recycling AI is 95%.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.r.a: It leaves out which photos the value came from. A reader could understand it as 95% in every situation.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.o.b: It got 95% on 200 test photos of clean new containers and 78% on 100 photos from the school bin.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.r.b: It wrote the conditions and the number of photos of both tests together so the reader can interpret the values.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.o.c: It was 78% on 100 photos from a school bin, so about 78% will come out in the bins of any other school too.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.r.c: It extended the result from 100 photos at one school to other schools. It did not check the condition of the containers at other schools.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.o.d: It was 78% on 100 bin photos, and 20 of the 22 wrong ones were containers that were crushed, labeled, or wet.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.r.d: Along with the result, it told the features of the wrong photos, honestly writing even where it is weak.
y-m-74-04.s.s2.explain: b and d state the conditions and number of the tested photos and do not say more than the results. a leaves out the conditions, and c generalizes to other schools.

y-m-74-05.title: If we use one more feature, how many more photos will we need?
y-m-74-05.topic: Number of features and amount of data needed
y-m-74-05.goal: Check that when the number of features grows, the number of divided cells grows by multiplication so the same data cannot fill the cells, and make several designs that fit the conditions and give reasons.
y-m-74-05.material:
A club is making an AI that classifies fruit in photos. The training photos available are 2,000. The values measured from a photo (things shown as numbers, such as weight, brightness of color, length) are called 'features'. The team decides on d features, divides each feature's values into b intervals, and then makes cells by pairing the intervals one by one. The number of cells is b multiplied d times (b^d, 'b to the d-th power'). For example, if b = 5 and d = 3, then 5×5×5 = 125 cells.
Agreement: each cell must have at least 5 photos on average for us to trust the judgment of that cell. Assume the photos are spread evenly over the cells.
y-m-74-05.thinking.0: Predicting and testing the rule of how the amount grows
y-m-74-05.thinking.2: Evaluating a colleague's proposal with numbers
y-m-74-05.prereq.0: The H1 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Only content up to middle-school math is assumed.
y-m-74-05.prereq.1: Reading and calculating powers (multiplying b by itself d times) (middle-school level)
y-m-74-05.prereq.2: Substituting numbers to check whether an inequality is true or false
y-m-74-05.s.s1.prompt: If you keep the number of intervals b = 5 and increase the features from 3 to 4, what happens to the number of cells?
y-m-74-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write down the number of cells yourself for d = 1, 2, 3 and look at the shape of the growth.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine how the intervals of the new feature get paired with each existing cell.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.o.a: One more feature is added, so cells increase by 5, to about 130 cells.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.r.a: You treated adding a feature as adding a cell. Think about how the intervals of the new feature are paired with every existing cell.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.o.b: When one more feature is attached, the cells multiply by the number of intervals, becoming 625 cells.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.r.b: You found the rule that the 5 intervals of the new feature pair with all the existing cells.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.o.c: The features went from 3 to 4, so the cells also become 4/3 times, about 167 cells.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.r.c: You thought the cells grow by the ratio of the number of features. The number of cells is determined by multiplying the number of intervals repeatedly, not in proportion to the number of features.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.o.d: Even if features increase, the cells stay the same and only more photos are needed.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.r.d: You thought the number of cells has nothing to do with the number of features. Draw how the way of dividing changes when you use one more feature.
y-m-74-05.s.s1.explain: In b^d, increasing d from 3 to 4 takes 5^3 = 125 to 5^4 = 625, growing by one more multiplication by the new feature's 5 intervals. With 5 photos per cell, you need 625 × 5 = 3,125 photos.
y-m-74-05.s.s2.prompt: With 2,000 photos, keeping 'at least 5 photos per cell on average', make 3 different designs (number of features d, number of intervals b) with at least 3 features and at least 3 intervals for each feature. d and b are natural numbers.

y-m-74-07.title: How many of 100 photos does 'probability 0.9 of being a cat' mean?
y-m-74-07.goal: Interpret the probability a model gives as the actual share of photos that received the same value, and revise your judgment and confidence while looking at data from several ranges.
y-m-74-07.material: A photo-classification AI gives each photo a 'probability of being a cat' as a number between 0 and 1. A person checked afterward whether each was really a cat. A probability of 0.9 can be read as meaning "if there are 100 photos that got the same number, about 90 of them are really cats." We want to find out whether this AI's probabilities can really be read that way.
y-m-74-07.thinking.0: Reading a probability as an actual ratio
y-m-74-07.thinking.1: Revising a judgment with new data
y-m-74-07.thinking.2: Comparing the validity of ways of checking
y-m-74-07.prereq.0: The H2 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Middle-school math and 'probability as a ratio' are assumed.
y-m-74-07.prereq.1: That probability is a ratio between 0 and 1 and can be read as 'about how many out of 100 times' (middle-school level)
y-m-74-07.s.s1.prompt: The data are revealed one piece at a time. Choose a judgment each time.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write on one line, side by side, the probability the AI stated and the actual share of cats.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.hint.1: Tell whether the new information changed your judgment or only changed the degree of confidence.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.info: There are 100 photos that the AI labeled 'probability 0.9 of being a cat'. We do not yet know how many are actually cats.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: About how many are actually cats?
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.after: You can read a probability of 0.9 as 'about 90 out of 100 similar photos', but you can only know whether this AI gives probabilities that can be trusted that way by counting.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Exactly 90. This is because 0.9 means 90 out of 100.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: A probability means 'about' that much. Declaring exactly 90 treats it as if there were no chance wobble.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It seems likely to be around 90, but we do not know whether this AI's probabilities can be trusted.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You stated together the expectation from reading the probability as a ratio and the condition that the expectation has not been confirmed.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Can't tell. 0.9 is just a score and has nothing to do with the number of photos.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: If a number is made as a probability, there is a way to read it as a ratio. It is a number whose correctness can be checked.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: All 100 are cats. This is because 0.9 is almost certain.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: 0.9 does not mean certain. It means there are photos that fall under the remaining 0.1.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.info: We checked the 100 photos one by one, and 70 were actually cats.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: How should we interpret this result?
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.after: The stated probability of 0.9 and the actual ratio of 0.7 do not match. This one batch alone cannot settle all the ranges, so we need to count the other ranges the same way.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is chance. 90 is right, and this time 20 fewer just happened to come out.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: A difference of 20 from the expected 90 is too big to see as a chance wobble. You can also check other batches in the same range.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 70 are cats, so we can just rewrite the probabilities of the other ranges as 0.7 too.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You applied the result of one range to all ranges. Each range must be checked separately.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The actual ratio for 0.9 is about 0.7. The probability in this range comes out high.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You compared the stated value with the actual ratio and read the AI's confidence as too strong. You must also remember that this is the result of this one batch only.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The AI was wrong in one range, so this AI's probabilities will be useless from now on.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: It is too early to conclude that every range is useless just because one range was off. You can find out by checking how the other ranges are.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.info:
We checked 100 photos in the other ranges too.
- Probability the AI stated 0.5: 48 actual cats
- Probability the AI stated 0.7: 61 actual cats
- Probability the AI stated 0.9: 70 actual cats
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the most fitting way to read the AI's probabilities from this table?
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.after: For the stated probabilities 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, the actual ratios are 0.48, 0.61, 0.70. The order is mostly kept, but in the high range the stated value is greater than the actual one. You should not trust the values as they are; you need calibration, which corrects them by reading the actual ratios.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The higher the stated probability, the higher the actual ratio generally is, but it is hard to trust the values as they are.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You told apart the tendency of the order and the mismatch of the values. The judgment is that the values must be calibrated before use.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The 0.5 range is closest to the actual ratio, so we throw away the results of the other ranges.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Throwing away the rest because only one range is right reduces the AI's usefulness too much. There is also the information that the higher range really is higher.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: In all three ranges, the probability the AI stated is the same as the actual share of cats.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: It is 70 in the 0.9 range and 61 in the 0.7 range, so they are not the same. Put the stated value and the actual ratio side by side for each range and compare.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The order of the stated probabilities cannot be trusted either. The difference between 0.7 and 0.9 means nothing.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: There is a flow in which, going 48 → 61 → 70, the higher the stated probability, the higher the actual ratio. The order carries information.
y-m-74-07.s.s1.reflect: How did your judgment and confidence change between when you first expected about 90 and after you saw the table? Why is it necessary to gather the photos that gave the same probability value and compare the actual ratio?
y-m-74-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose everything that is a fitting way to check whether the AI's probabilities can be trusted.
y-m-74-07.s.s2.hint.0: Tell apart whether what you want to check is 'whether one photo is right' or 'how many of many photos are right'.
y-m-74-07.s.s2.hint.1: Compare how stable the actual ratio would be when a batch has 10 photos and when it has 1,000.
y-m-74-07.s.s2.o.a: Gather the photos that gave the same probability value into one batch and compare with the actual ratio
y-m-74-07.s.s2.r.a: This is a method of comparing the stated probability and the actual ratio side by side in the same batch.
y-m-74-07.s.s2.o.b: Find the single share correct over all photos (accuracy) and see whether it equals the probability
y-m-74-07.s.s2.r.b: A single accuracy figure hides the differences between probability ranges. Even if the 0.9 range is off and the 0.5 range is right, it may not show up in the average.
y-m-74-07.s.s2.o.c: Pick one photo shown with a probability of 0.9 and look at whether it is really a cat
y-m-74-07.s.s2.r.c: Whether that one photo is a cat or not, you cannot know the ratio. You need many photos.
y-m-74-07.s.s2.o.d: Also check that each batch has enough photos so the ratio does not wobble by chance
y-m-74-07.s.s2.r.d: If a batch is small, the ratio wobbles a lot. This is a check that also looks at that degree.
y-m-74-07.s.s2.explain: a is a method of directly comparing the stated probability with the actual ratio, and d is a method of checking that the comparison does not wobble by chance. b hides the differences between ranges, and c cannot give a ratio from a single photo.

y-m-74-08.title: Is the curve with training error 0 the most trustworthy?
y-m-74-08.goal: Choose a model by comparing the error on the training data with the error on new data, and find and explain the reasoning mistake of trusting a model just because its training error is small.
y-m-74-08.material:
There are the study times and test scores of 20 students. A model was made from the data of 10 of them (training data), and performance on new data was checked with the data of the other 10 (validation data). The mean squared errors (the average of the squared errors; the smaller, the better) of the three models are as follows.
- Model A (straight line): training 12.0, validation 13.5
- Model B (cubic curve): training 4.5, validation 6.0
- Model C (9th-degree curve): training 0.0, validation 41.0
Model C is a wiggly curve that passes exactly through all 10 points of the training data.
y-m-74-08.thinking.0: Comparing models by putting the two kinds of error together
y-m-74-08.thinking.1: Finding wrong reasoning in an argument
y-m-74-08.thinking.2: Adjusting confidence to the amount of evidence
y-m-74-08.prereq.0: The H2 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Middle-school math and 'probability as a ratio' are assumed.
y-m-74-08.prereq.1: Reading that the smaller the mean of the squared errors (mean squared error), the closer the predictions (the values are given)
y-m-74-08.prereq.2: A sense for comparing how well a straight line and a curve pass through the points
y-m-74-08.s.s1.prompt: Which model would you choose to predict the score of a new student next semester?
y-m-74-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put the training errors and validation errors of the three models side by side in a table.
y-m-74-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the difference between the two errors differs for each model.
y-m-74-08.s.s1.o.a: Model C — its error on the training data is 0, so it is the most accurate model
y-m-74-08.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at the error on the training data. Look at how you can explain the error of 41.0 on new data.
y-m-74-08.s.s1.o.b: Model A — it is the simplest so it is easy to explain, and its error is not very bad either
y-m-74-08.s.s1.r.b: Simplicity is a reasonable standard. But the validation error of 13.5 is more than twice Model B's 6.0.
y-m-74-08.s.s1.o.c: Model B — both the training and validation errors are small, and the difference between them is small too
y-m-74-08.s.s1.r.c: You compared the training data and new data together.
y-m-74-08.s.s1.o.d: Choose none — there are only 10 validation data, so no model can be compared
y-m-74-08.s.s1.r.d: With little data your confidence decreases, but there are big differences among the three: 41.0, 13.5, and 6.0. It is not that comparison is impossible.
y-m-74-08.s.s1.explain: Model B has the smallest validation error, 6.0, and its difference from the training error is small, 1.5. Model C has a training error of 0, but its validation error of 41.0 is the largest.
y-m-74-08.s.s1.acc.0: If being easy to explain is the most important in the situation, you can choose A. But by the error standard, B shows a smaller value on new data.
y-m-74-08.s.s2.prompt: A student wrote the explanation in the presentation like this. Choose the line whose thinking is wrong.
y-m-74-08.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether the evidence in line 2 is a result on the training data or a result on new data.
y-m-74-08.s.s2.hint.1: Compare how that evidence does not fit the numbers in line 3.
y-m-74-08.s.s2.line.0: The training errors are 12.0 for A, 4.5 for B, and 0.0 for C, so they decrease as the curve gets more complicated.
y-m-74-08.s.s2.line.1: C passes through all the points of the training data, so it is the model that found the pattern in the data most accurately.
y-m-74-08.s.s2.line.2: But on new data, C's error is 41.0, the largest of the three models.
y-m-74-08.s.s2.line.3: It may be because C followed even the chance wobbles in the training data.
y-m-74-08.s.s2.line.4: So when choosing a model, you must also look at the error on new data.
y-m-74-08.s.s2.explain: Line 2 is the mistake. Passing through all the points of the training data can mean that it memorized the training data, so it is not evidence that it found the pattern. The error on new data (41.0) shows that.

y-m-74-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the judgment I wrote tied to the error numbers (6.0, 13.5, 41.0, etc.)?
y-m-74-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about whether what you would do further would really raise confidence?

y-m-74-09.title: An email with both 'free' and 'prize' in it: how suspicious is it?
y-m-74-09.topic: Spam filters and the independence assumption
y-m-74-09.goal: Learn the assumption that to multiply the probabilities of two words, the two words must not influence each other within spam, make possible cases where the assumption breaks, and say what more must be known to reach a conclusion.
y-m-74-09.material:
A spam filter looks at the words in an email and judges whether it is spam. Collecting 100 spam emails, 50 contained 'free' and 40 contained 'prize'. Among 100 normal emails, 3 contained 'free' and 2 contained 'prize'.
The developer wants to continue the calculation assuming that "0.2, the product of the ratio 0.5 at which 'free' appears in spam and the ratio 0.4 at which 'prize' appears, is the ratio at which the two words appear together." (This is the same as assuming that 20 of the 100 spam emails contain both words.)
y-m-74-09.thinking.0: Finding the hidden assumption of a calculation
y-m-74-09.thinking.1: Making possible cases (counterexamples) where the assumption breaks
y-m-74-09.thinking.2: Saying what information is needed for the conclusion
y-m-74-09.prereq.0: The H2 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Middle-school math and 'probability as a ratio' are assumed.
y-m-74-09.prereq.1: Knowing that probability is a ratio from 0 to 1, and reading how often two words appear together by splitting into a table with four cells
y-m-74-09.prereq.2: Reading the possible range with inequalities
y-m-74-09.s.s1.prompt: For this multiplication (0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2) to be correct, how must the two words appear within spam emails?
y-m-74-09.s.s1.hint.0: Draw a table that splits the 100 spam emails into four cells: 'free' present/absent and 'prize' present/absent.
y-m-74-09.s.s1.hint.1: Write down what the number of emails in each cell would be if the multiplication is correct.
y-m-74-09.s.s1.o.a: Whether or not 'free' is present, the ratio at which 'prize' appears within spam is the same
y-m-74-09.s.s1.r.a: This says in terms of ratios that the two words do not influence each other.
y-m-74-09.s.s1.o.b: It always holds if 50 spam emails contain 'free' and 40 contain 'prize'
y-m-74-09.s.s1.r.b: The counts of the two words alone do not decide the count of emails that contain both. Even with the same counts, how often they appear together can differ.
y-m-74-09.s.s1.o.c: In normal emails too, 'free' must appear at a ratio of 0.5 and 'prize' at 0.4
y-m-74-09.s.s1.r.c: The ratios in normal emails are separate from the calculation within spam. The condition under which this multiplication is correct is about the relationship within spam emails.
y-m-74-09.s.s1.o.d: It holds only if not a single spam email contains both words
y-m-74-09.s.s1.r.d: If no spam email contains both, that actually contradicts the product 0.2.
y-m-74-09.s.s1.explain: For the product of the two ratios to be used as the 'ratio of appearing together', whether one word is present or not must not affect the ratio at which the other word appears. This is called independence.
y-m-74-09.s.s2.prompt: Keep as they are the 50 of 100 spam emails with 'free' and the 40 with 'prize', and decide the number x of spam emails that contain both words. Make 3 different values of x that differ from the multiplication assumption (20) and are actually possible. (x is an integer of at least 0.)
y-m-74-09.s.s2.hint.0: Place the 40 emails with 'prize' first, and think about the cases where the fewest and the most of them also contain 'free'.
y-m-74-09.s.s2.hint.1: Check that even adding the 50 emails with 'free' and the 40 emails with 'prize' does not exceed 100.
y-m-74-09.s.s2.var.x: Number x of spam emails containing both words
y-m-74-09.s.s2.ok.c1: x is an integer of at least 0.
y-m-74-09.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be an integer of at least 0.
y-m-74-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The emails containing both do not exceed the 40 containing 'prize'.
y-m-74-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The emails containing both cannot be more than the 40 containing 'prize'.
y-m-74-09.s.s2.ok.c3: It differs from the multiplication assumption's 20.
y-m-74-09.s.s2.fail.c3: If x is 20, it is the same as the multiplication assumption. Pick another value.
y-m-74-09.s.s2.explain: The 50 and the 40 fit within 100, so the number of emails containing both can be anything from 0 to 40. The multiplication assumption is just one case among them, 20. For example, if all the emails with 'prize' also contain 'free', then x = 40.
y-m-74-09.s.s3.prompt: Can the probability that an email containing both words is spam be decided with only the information we have now? If it cannot, write what more must be known.
y-m-74-09.s.s3.hint.0: Think about what is missing if you know only the number containing both in spam.
y-m-74-09.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the information that normal emails among 100 have 3 and 2 with 'free' and 'prize' respectively lets you know the number containing both.
y-m-74-09.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Can it be decided? ... must be known.
y-m-74-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you talk about both the spam side and the normal side?
y-m-74-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart the 'ratio appearing separately' and the 'number appearing together'?
y-m-74-09.s.s3.model.0: It can't be decided. You need to know both the number of emails with both words among the 100 spam and the number with both among the 100 normal emails to compare.
y-m-74-09.s.s3.model.1: To find the probability of spam, you need to know how many emails have 'free' and 'prize' appearing together in both spam and normal emails. The ratios of appearing separately are not enough.

y-m-74-10.title: B has the smaller average error, so why do some people say A is better?
y-m-74-10.goal: Check by making your own case that the ranking of two models can flip depending on the measure that summarizes error (average error size, mean of squared errors), and choose a model based on the measure that fits the situation.
y-m-74-10.material:
A delivery app compares models A and B that predict arrival time. For the same 5 deliveries, the difference between the prediction and the actual time (error; unit minutes; only the size, without the sign) is as follows.
- Model A: 3, 3, 3, 3, 3
- Model B: 1, 1, 1, 1, 9
We compare with two measures. Average error size = the average of the error sizes, mean square = the average of the values obtained by squaring each error. For both measures, the smaller, the better the model.
One team member says, "B's average error size is smaller, so B is better."
y-m-74-10.thinking.0: Testing whether a measure can change the ranking
y-m-74-10.thinking.1: Making a case yourself that fits the conditions
y-m-74-10.thinking.2: Choosing the measure that fits the purpose of the service
y-m-74-10.prereq.0: The H2 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Middle-school math and 'probability as a ratio' are assumed.
y-m-74-10.prereq.1: Calculating absolute value, average, and squares (middle-school level)
y-m-74-10.prereq.2: A sense for comparing collections of numbers that have a fixed sum but a different spread
y-m-74-10.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting response to the team member's statement?
y-m-74-10.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the average error size and the mean square of the two models and write them in a table.
y-m-74-10.s.s1.explain: The average error size is 3 for A and 2.6 for B, so B is smaller. The mean square is 9 for A and (1+1+1+1+81)÷5 = 17 for B, so A is smaller. A measure that weighs large errors more heavily and one that does not can rank them differently.
y-m-74-10.s.s2.prompt: Keep A's errors at 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, and decide a new model B's 5 errors (b1 to b5, numbers from 0 to 20) so that 'the average error size is smaller than A's and the mean square is larger than A's', and make 3 different B's. Ones that only change the order of the errors count as the same B.
y-m-74-10.s.s2.hint.0: First test what happens to the two measures if all 5 errors are the same value.
y-m-74-10.s.s2.hint.1: Test how the sum of squares changes if you keep the sum nearly the same and make only one error bigger.
y-m-74-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The average error size is smaller than A's 3.
y-m-74-10.s.s2.fail.c2: The average error size is not smaller than 3. Check the sum of the five errors divided by 5.
y-m-74-10.s.s2.ok.c3: The mean square is larger than A's 9.
y-m-74-10.s.s2.fail.c3: The mean square is not larger than 9. Check the sum of the squared errors divided by 5.
y-m-74-10.s.s2.explain: B = (1, 1, 1, 1, 9) has an average error size of 2.6 and a mean square of 17. Similarly, keep the sum less than 15 while making one error big so the sum of squares goes over 45. A model that concentrates the error in one place is this kind of case.
y-m-74-10.s.s3.prompt: The delivery app says it most wants to avoid 'occasionally being badly late'. Write which of A and B you would choose, and which measure helps that choice, with reasons.
y-m-74-10.s.s3.hint.0: Compare how many minutes the latest case is for A and for B.
y-m-74-10.s.s3.hint.1: Look at the formulas of the two measures to find which measure reflects that difference more.
y-m-74-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the model I chose connect to the goal of 'occasionally being badly late'?
y-m-74-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about whether the choice would differ for a different goal (such as most deliveries needing to be roughly accurate)?
y-m-74-10.s.s3.model.0: I would choose A. The mean square is 9 for A and 17 for B; B is wrong by as much as 9 minutes once, so it sometimes is badly late. A measure that weighs large errors more heavily fits this situation.
y-m-74-10.s.s3.model.1: A is safer than B. B's average error size is small, 2.6, but it has one 9-minute error, so it can sometimes be badly late. So I would look at the mean square, which is sensitive to large errors.

y-m-74-11.title: Is a split with one side completely clean always the better split?
y-m-74-11.topic: Comparing splits in a decision tree
y-m-74-11.goal: Check that the sizes of the two nodes must be taken into account when comparing impurity after a split, by finding and fixing the wrong line in a worked calculation, and make several splits that meet the condition.
y-m-74-11.material:
We want to choose a rule (split) that divides 20 emails (10 spam, 10 normal) into two groups. The 'impurity' of a group is measured as 1 − (spam ratio)² − (normal ratio)². It is 0 if there is only one kind, and 0.5, the largest, if it is half and half. The smaller the impurity after splitting, the better the split.
- Split X: left 10 emails (spam 8, normal 2), right 10 emails (spam 2, normal 8)
- Split Z: left 2 emails (spam 2, normal 0), right 18 emails (spam 8, normal 10)
How to combine the impurity of the whole after splitting into a single value is for you to work out as you solve the problem.
y-m-74-11.thinking.0: Checking an intuitive judgment with calculation
y-m-74-11.thinking.1: Finding wrong reasoning in a solution
y-m-74-11.thinking.2: Making several splits that meet the condition
y-m-74-11.prereq.0: The H2 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Middle-school math and 'probability as a ratio' are assumed.
y-m-74-11.prereq.1: Calculating with ratios and squares (middle-school level)
y-m-74-11.s.s1.prompt: Before calculating, which of splits X and Z do you think split the parent (spam 10, normal 10) better?
y-m-74-11.s.s1.hint.0: First write how many emails are in each of the two groups in each split.
y-m-74-11.s.s1.o.c: Hard to say before calculating — you must consider the sizes and impurities of the two groups together
y-m-74-11.s.s1.r.c: This is an attitude of not deciding by intuition alone but checking with calculation.
y-m-74-11.s.s1.explain: In split X, 18 of the 20 emails are the kind that dominates its own group. In split Z, the clean group has only 2 emails. If you calculate, X's impurity is smaller.
y-m-74-11.s.s1.acc.0: An attitude of putting off intuition and checking with calculation is also fitting. The calculation shows that X has the smaller impurity.
y-m-74-11.s.s2.prompt: A student calculated the two splits and organized them as below. Choose the line whose thinking is wrong.
y-m-74-11.s.s2.line.0: Parent group: spam 10, normal 10, so the impurity = 1 − 0.5² − 0.5² = 0.5.
y-m-74-11.s.s2.line.1: Split X: the left impurity is 0.32 and the right impurity is 0.32.
y-m-74-11.s.s2.line.2: Split Z: the left (spam 2, normal 0) impurity is 0, and the right (spam 8, normal 10) impurity is about 0.494.
y-m-74-11.s.s2.line.3: Let's take the impurity after splitting as the average of the two groups' values. X is 0.32, and Z is (0 + 0.494) ÷ 2 ≈ 0.247.
y-m-74-11.s.s2.line.4: 0.247 is smaller, so Z is the better split.
y-m-74-11.s.s2.explain: Line 4 is the mistake. The groups differ in size, but the two values were averaged equally. Combining them with weights by the number of emails gives X as 0.32 and Z as (2×0 + 18×0.494) ÷ 20 ≈ 0.444. Then the conclusion in line 5 changes too, and X is the better split.
y-m-74-11.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different splits whose impurity after splitting is smaller than X's 0.32. Put a spam and b normal emails in the left group, and all the rest go to the right group. (a and b are integers from 0 to 10, and neither group may be empty.) Splits that swap left and right are the same split.
y-m-74-11.s.s3.hint.0: Pick an a and b, find the number of emails and the impurity of each of the two groups, and combine them using weights.
y-m-74-11.s.s3.hint.1: Compare what value you get from a split in which both groups have one side dominant, versus one clean group.
y-m-74-11.s.s3.ok.c1: a and b are integers from 0 to 10.
y-m-74-11.s.s3.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from 0 to 10.
y-m-74-11.s.s3.fail.c2: One of the left and right groups is empty.
y-m-74-11.s.s3.ok.c3: The impurity after splitting is smaller than 0.32.
y-m-74-11.s.s3.fail.c3: The impurity after splitting is not smaller than 0.32. Find the combined value taking the sizes of the groups into account.
y-m-74-11.s.s3.explain: For example, (a, b) = (9, 1) gives left (spam 9, normal 1) and right (spam 1, normal 9), so the impurity after splitting is 0.18. With (10, 0), both groups have only one kind, so it is 0. Z, which is (2, 0), is about 0.444, larger than 0.32.

y-m-74-12.title: Can we write 'B is better' because B got 2 more questions right?
y-m-74-12.topic: Model comparison and the number of test questions
y-m-74-12.goal: Check with a question-by-question comparison table that a small difference in test results can be due to chance, and rewrite this result as a sentence that tells readers without exaggeration.
y-m-74-12.material: The club had models A and B solve the same 50-question test. A got 43 questions (86%) right and B got 45 questions (90%) right. The club president says, "Let's write 'B is better than A' in the newsletter." The newsletter is read by school friends who don't know much about AI.
y-m-74-12.thinking.0: Assessing the strength of evidence for a small difference
y-m-74-12.thinking.1: Finding overstated claims in an argument
y-m-74-12.prereq.0: The H2 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Middle-school math and 'probability as a ratio' are assumed.
y-m-74-12.prereq.1: Reading accuracy = number correct ÷ total number as a percentage
y-m-74-12.prereq.2: Filling in the cells of a table (both right / both wrong, etc.) and adding them up to match the total
y-m-74-12.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting judgment on writing 'B is better than A' in the newsletter based on this result alone?
y-m-74-12.s.s1.hint.0: Turn the accuracy difference into a number of questions.
y-m-74-12.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the result could be different if the test had 50 different questions.
y-m-74-12.s.s1.o.a: You can write it. B got 2 more right, so B is better.
y-m-74-12.s.s1.r.a: You did not consider that the 2-question difference may be the result of which questions happened to be chosen for this test.
y-m-74-12.s.s1.explain: A 4%p accuracy difference corresponds to 2 questions. If tested with different questions, the difference could shrink or the order could flip. To write it in the newsletter, this must be told along with it.
y-m-74-12.s.s2.prompt: The president compared question by question and explained it as below. Choose the line whose thinking is wrong.
y-m-74-12.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether adding all four cells of the table gives 50.
y-m-74-12.s.s2.hint.1: Collect separately the questions where the two models' results differ and count how many there are.
y-m-74-12.s.s2.line.0: A got 43 of the 50 questions right, and B got 45.
y-m-74-12.s.s2.line.1: Looking question by question, 42 questions were answered right by both models and 4 questions were wrong for both.
y-m-74-12.s.s2.line.2: The remaining 4 questions split, with 3 questions only B got right and 1 question only A got right.
y-m-74-12.s.s2.line.3: The questions only B got right are 3 times those only A got right, so this difference cannot be chance, and B is definitely the better model.
y-m-74-12.s.s2.line.4: So let's write 'B is better than A' in the newsletter.
y-m-74-12.s.s2.explain: Line 4 is the mistake. Only 4 questions had split results, and they just split 3 to 1. The probability of getting heads 3 or more times in 4 tosses of a fair coin is 5/16 (about 31%), so a difference this size often arises by chance too. The conclusion in line 5 also lacks grounds.
y-m-74-12.s.s3.prompt: For the friends who will read the newsletter (they don't know AI terms well), rewrite this result without exaggerating it. Include at least one number, and separate what this result tells us from what we do not know yet.
y-m-74-12.s.s3.hint.0: Think about what you need to say so that friends reading it do not say 'so let's use B'.
y-m-74-12.s.s3.hint.1: Write it split into one line for what we learned and one line for what we do not know yet.
y-m-74-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write it so that a friend reading it does not misunderstand that 'B is definitely better'?
y-m-74-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the numbers I wrote match the numbers in the text?
y-m-74-12.s.s3.model.0: On the 50-question test, A got 43 questions right and B got 45. B looks like it did a little better, but only 4 questions had different results, so it could be chance. It is still hard to say B is better, and we plan to test again with more questions.
y-m-74-12.s.s3.model.1: When they solved the same 50 questions, A got 86% right and B got 90%. But this difference is only 2 questions, so it could be chance. For now we see the two models as similar, and we will check again with more questions.

y-m-74-13.title: If each step is 80 to 95%, what is the overall success rate of a 4-step assistant?
y-m-74-13.topic: Overall success rate of a multi-step AI
y-m-74-13.goal: Check by prediction that the overall success rate of a system with several steps in a row is set by the product of the step success rates, and design several sets of step accuracies that meet a target success rate and explain why.
y-m-74-13.material:
A voice assistant goes through 4 steps from hearing speech to answering. The accuracy of each step is 'the share of the time this step is also right when all the earlier steps were right'.
① Turning sound into text 95%
② Finding out the type of request from the text 90%
③ Finding the needed information 90%
④ Making a fitting answer 80%
Agreement: if even one step is wrong, the whole thing counts as a failure, and a mistake does not fix itself in a later step.
y-m-74-13.thinking.0: Estimating the overall success rate from the accuracy of each step
y-m-74-13.thinking.1: Making several designs that satisfy the constraints
y-m-74-13.thinking.2: Explaining why the whole shrinks as steps are added
y-m-74-13.prereq.0: The H2 label in this batch only distinguishes the difficulty and support level of the production batch; it does not mean this subject is assigned to a particular grade. Middle-school math and 'probability as a ratio' are assumed.
y-m-74-13.prereq.1: Following, with a concrete number such as 100 requests, how many are left after each step
y-m-74-13.s.s1.prompt: Which is the closest to the share of the time this 4-step assistant answers correctly all the way through?
y-m-74-13.s.s1.hint.0: Suppose there are 100 requests and write in turn how many are left after each step.
y-m-74-13.s.s1.hint.1: Compare why adding up the share that go wrong and applying the share that remain one after another are different methods.
y-m-74-13.s.s1.o.a: About 80% — it cannot exceed the accuracy of the lowest step, so it is near that
y-m-74-13.s.s1.r.a: It is true that the lowest step is the upper limit of the whole. You did not reflect that the failures of the other steps add up.
y-m-74-13.s.s1.o.b: About 89% — it is the average of the four steps' accuracies
y-m-74-13.s.s1.r.b: The average is the average level when one step is right. It is different from the share that succeed only by passing through all four steps.
y-m-74-13.s.s1.o.c: About 62% — it is the value from applying the next step's share in turn to the share that were right in the previous step
y-m-74-13.s.s1.r.c: You estimated by applying the next step's accuracy to the share remaining after each step.
y-m-74-13.s.s1.o.d: About 55% — it is 100 minus the sum of the wrong shares 5, 10, 10, 20%
y-m-74-13.s.s1.r.d: You added the wrong shares and subtracted them. Once something is already wrong, the next step's failure does not happen separately, so this method counts failures overlapping.
y-m-74-13.s.s1.explain: Of 100, the 95 that pass ① are cut to 90% at ②, leaving 85.5, then 76.95 at ③, and 61.56 at ④. 0.95 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.6156, so it is about 62%.
y-m-74-13.s.s2.prompt: Now we design a three-step assistant. Decide each step's accuracy (%, an integer) and make 3 different combinations for which the overall success rate is at least 90%. Each step's accuracy is from 50% to 99%. The same values in a different order count as the same combination.
y-m-74-13.s.s2.hint.0: First find the minimum accuracy needed when all three steps have the same value.
y-m-74-13.s.s2.hint.1: If you lower one step, test by changing values how much higher the other two steps must be.
y-m-74-13.s.s2.fail.c1: Please enter the accuracy as an integer (%).
y-m-74-13.s.s2.fail.c2: Each step must be from 50% to 99%.
y-m-74-13.s.s2.ok.c3: The overall success rate is at least 90%.
y-m-74-13.s.s2.fail.c3: The overall success rate falls short of 90%. Check by multiplying the three accuracies divided by 100.
y-m-74-13.s.s2.explain: (99, 99, 92) gives 0.99 × 0.99 × 0.92 ≈ 0.9017, and (97, 97, 97) gives ≈ 0.9127. (95, 95, 95) gives ≈ 0.857, which falls short of the target. If one step is low, the other steps must be very high.
y-m-74-13.s.s3.prompt: What happens to the overall success rate if you attach one more 97% step to the assistant whose three steps are all 97% (about 91.3% overall)? Using numbers, explain why the whole goes down even though every step is as high as 97%.
y-m-74-13.s.s3.hint.0: First write how many of 100 requests remain after 3 steps.
y-m-74-13.s.s3.hint.1: Then write how many the remaining requests become after passing the new step.
y-m-74-13.s.s3.placeholder: Example: It was about 91.3% with 3 steps, and when one more step is attached ...
y-m-74-13.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the number I wrote lead to a value reduced from 91.3%?
y-m-74-13.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the agreement that 'all must be right to succeed' in the reason?
y-m-74-13.s.s3.model.0: The more steps there are, the more we keep multiplying by a number less than 1, because all must be right to succeed. Multiplying by 0.97 once more shrinks 0.913 to about 0.885, so it becomes about 88.5%.
y-m-74-13.s.s3.model.1: If even one is wrong, the whole is wrong, so the chances to go wrong increase. To the success rate of about 91.3% at 3 steps, one more step is added and only 97% of it remains, so it becomes about 88.5%.
